summary: This document describes how to optimize ARP and Neighbor Discovery traffic in a TRILL campus. TRILL switches keep a cache of IP, MAC and Data Label bindings learned from ARP and ND messages and can answer from it, which reduces broadcast traffic.

eli5.summary: Instead of shouting to the whole room, who has this address, a helper who already knows the answer replies directly.

questions: how to reduce arp traffic in trill
how to reduce arp flooding in trill
how does trill handle duplicate ip addresses
subtitle: How TRILL edge switches answer ARP and Neighbor Discovery queries from a cache instead of flooding them.

tldr.problem: ARP is normally broadcast and ND is normally multicast, so on a TRILL campus these multi-destination queries and answers get flooded to many switches.
tldr.mechanism: Edge RBridges keep a cache of IP/MAC/Data Label bindings learned from ARP/ND, DHCP and directories, and then reply directly, unicast the query to the target's egress RBridge, or fall back to flooding.
tldr.outcome: Flooding of ARP/ND traffic is reduced, and with complete address information it could be suppressed entirely. The mechanism is optional for RBridges.

facts.label: Cache entry
facts.value: {IP address, MAC address, ingress nickname} per Data Label

facts.label: Default ageing timer
facts.value: 3/4 of the MAC learning ageing timer

today: RFC 8302 is a Standards Track document and, per the unit metadata, it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Flooding Problem
sections.content:
ARP and ND messages are normally sent by broadcast and multicast, respectively. In a TRILL campus, such multi-destination messages burden the network. RBridges MAY therefore implement an optimized ARP/ND response when the target's location is known by the ingress RBridge or can be obtained from a directory.

The RFC points to RFC 6820 for the issues that IP address resolution can cause in data centers because of flooded packets. A proxy ARP/ND function on edge RBridges avoids that flooding.
sections.eli5: Normally asking who has an address means shouting to everyone. A switch that already knows the answer can reply, so nobody else has to hear the shout.

sections.title: Learning IP and MAC Bindings
sections.content:
Edge RBridges can learn an end station's IP/MAC mapping in three ways: manual configuration through management, control-plane mechanisms such as directories (RFC 8171), or data-plane snooping of ARP/ND, DHCP or gratuitous ARP messages.

A cache entry is a triplet of {IP address, MAC address, ingress nickname} for a given Data Label (a VLAN or a Fine-Grained Label). By default an RBridge only learns MAC and Data Label to nickname mappings from data frames. The IA APPsub-TLV (RFC 7961) lets any RBridge distribute IP/MAC mappings in the control plane, for example inside ESADI (RFC 7357). Its Flags field tells whether the source is a directory server or local observation, and a confidence level can indicate how reliable a mapping is.

Most hosts announce themselves right after coming online with DHCP, gratuitous ARP or RARP, so the local edge RBridge usually learns them immediately and shares them with other edge RBridges.
sections.eli5: Each helper keeps an address book of who lives where. They learn entries by listening to hosts introduce themselves, and by sharing notes with other helpers.

sections.title: How an Ingress RBridge Replies
sections.content:
An ARP message is recognized by Ethertype 0x0806, and ND by being one of five ICMPv6 packet types. For a generic request where the ingress RBridge knows the target's IP and MAC, it MUST take one or a combination of these actions:

  • Reply directly to the querier from its cache, using the target's address as the ND source IP.
  • Encapsulate the request to the target's Designated RBridge so the target answers authoritatively.
  • Hold back repeated requests for the same target and answer when the recent query is answered.
  • Reply from directory information (Pull or Push Directory).
  • Flood the request as per RFC 6325.

If the target is unknown, the RBridge MUST flood, pull from a directory server and reply, or drop the message when the directory authoritatively says the address does not exist. Gratuitous ARP and unsolicited Neighbor Advertisements may be shared with an IA APPsub-TLV, and SHOULD be discarded when complete Push Directory information is in use. Address probes and DAD Neighbor Solicitations SHOULD be handled like generic requests.

When the request goes to the egress RBridge R2, R2 asks on the target's link and unicasts the response back to R1, which passes it to the querier. R2 SHOULD also announce the target's location and addresses to the other RBridges.
sections.eli5: The helper can answer from its address book, ask the right neighbor to check, wait for an answer already on its way, or as a last resort shout to everyone.

sections.title: SEND, RARP and DHCP
sections.content:
Secure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) messages need cryptographic keys, and the RFC leaves key distribution to RBridges out of scope. RBridges therefore do not construct SEND messages and are generally transparent to them, although they SHOULD snoop on SEND to extract addressing information. A local reply is impossible because the RBridge cannot sign with the target's private key, so only forwarding to the target or flooding is valid.

RARP uses the ARP packet format with Ethertype 0x8035 and different opcodes, and asks for the IP address for a given MAC address. It SHOULD be answered by a local cache or directory lookup on the hardware address. For DHCP, an edge RBridge should snoop the exchange, mainly the DHCPAck, store the mapping and send it out over ESADI.
sections.eli5: Some letters are sealed with a signature, so the helper cannot answer for the person and just passes them along. For reverse questions, who has this MAC, the helper checks the book the other way round.

sections.title: Duplicates, Ageing and Mobility
sections.content:
Duplicate IP addresses can come from fake ARP/ND messages or configuration mistakes. With complete trustworthy directory information, any appearance of an IP elsewhere is by definition incorrect. Without it, the optimization should support duplicate detection, which is critical in a data center to stop spoofing from diverting traffic. An RBridge may send a unicast DAD-query to the former owner of an address; if the former owner replies, the querier SHOULD log the duplicate for the administrator. If there is no answer in a given time, it may be mobility and the new entry is confirmed.

Dynamic entries MUST be removed if the link they were learned on fails, and SHOULD be flushed when not refreshed within the age-time. The IP/MAC ageing timer is configurable per RBridge and defaults to 3/4 of the MAC address learning ageing timer. When an end station moves from RB1 to RB2, RB2 advertises it and the old entry on RB1 SHOULD be replaced. An RBridge MAY probe an end station periodically so entries refresh before they age out.
sections.eli5: If two people claim the same address, the helper politely asks the old owner. And entries in the address book get crossed out when they are not used for a while or when someone moves.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There are two ways to learn the address information: data-plane mode (traditional bridge learning) and directory mode. In data-plane mode the answers RBridges give are generally those the end stations would give anyway, so the security considerations are those of ARP/ND. Unless SEND is used, ARP and ND can be easily forged, so learning from them is hackable. Link security such as IEEE 802.1AE between end stations and edge RBridges could help, but it is beyond scope and would impose requirements on end stations.

With trustworthy and complete directory information, responses can rely entirely on it, which bounds the damage forged messages can do to the local link. Where directory data is incomplete, the confidence level in the IA APPsub-TLV can arbitrate between sources. RBridges should rate limit ARP/ND queries injected into the campus to limit some denial-of-service attacks.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write a fake name in the address book unless there is a signature check. A trusted, complete directory limits how much trouble a faker can cause.

viz.caption: WAYS AN INGRESS RBRIDGE CAN ANSWER A KNOWN TARGET (RFC 8302)

items.title: Reply from cache
items.text: Answer the querier directly using the cached MAC.

items.title: Unicast to egress
items.text: Encapsulate the query to the target's Designated RBridge.

items.title: Hold and relay
items.text: Block repeats and answer when the pending query is answered.

items.title: Directory reply
items.text: Answer from Pull or Push Directory data.

items.title: Flood
items.text: Fall back to flooding as per RFC 6325.
